890:
Appeasement is the act of giving an aggressive, threatening, or demanding person or group what they want — not because it's fair or right — but specifically to calm them down, avoid a fight, or prevent a bigger conflict from breaking out.

The key word here is concession. A concession means you give something up — a right, a territory, a principle, something valuable — that you otherwise wouldn't give up. Appeasement is when you make that sacrifice specifically to satisfy an aggressor, hoping they'll stop being hostile.

A simple everyday image: imagine a school bully demands your lunch money. You hand it over so they won't hit you. You haven't solved the problem — you've just bought temporary peace by giving in. That's appeasement.

The word "appeasement" is deeply tied to one of the most famous (and catastrophic) moments in modern history: the Munich Agreement of 1938.

Adolf Hitler, the leader of Nazi Germany, was aggressively demanding that a region of Czechoslovakia called the Sudetenland be handed over to Germany. Instead of resisting, British Prime Minister Neville Chamberlain and French leaders agreed to give Hitler what he wanted. Their reasoning: satisfying this demand would prevent a larger war. Chamberlain returned home famously announcing he had secured "peace for our time."

It was a disaster. Within months, Hitler invaded the rest of Czechoslovakia. Within a year, World War II had begun — the deadliest conflict in human history. The Munich Agreement became the world's defining example of appeasement gone catastrophically wrong, and it is why the word carries such heavy weight and such a strong negative meaning today.

The core problem with appeasement is what it signals to the aggressor. When you give in to threats:

  • You reward aggressive behavior, teaching the aggressor that threats work
  • You invite more demands, because they now know you'll yield when pressured
  • You weaken your own position, because others see you as unable or unwilling to stand firm
  • You often delay the conflict rather than prevent it — and the delayed version is usually worse

This is why appeasement is generally seen as shortsighted. It trades long-term security for short-term quiet.

In modern usage, calling something "appeasement" is almost always a criticism. It implies weakness, cowardice, or a failure of nerve — that someone is sacrificing principles or safety just to avoid discomfort right now.

If a leader says "We will not engage in appeasement with terrorist groups," they're saying: we refuse to reward threats by giving in to demands, no matter how much pressure is applied.
Appeasement vs. Compromise — An Important Distinction

These two words can seem similar, but they're quite different:

Compromise is mutual. Both sides give something up, both sides gain something. It's a balanced exchange arrived at through negotiation between relative equals. Neither side is under a serious threat.

Appeasement is one-sided. One party keeps demanding; the other keeps giving — typically out of fear, weakness, or a desperate desire to avoid conflict. The aggressor gives nothing meaningful in return. There's an inherent imbalance of power or threat.

So when people criticize a negotiation as "appeasement," they're saying it wasn't a real compromise — it was just caving.

The word isn't only for wars and politics. It shows up in ordinary life too:

  • A manager who never disciplines a difficult, disruptive employee because they dread confrontation
  • Parents who hand a screaming child candy every time they throw a tantrum in a store
  • A person who constantly agrees with a domineering partner — not because they genuinely agree, but to avoid an argument

In every case, the short-term payoff is peace and quiet. The long-term cost is that the difficult person becomes bolder, learns that bad behavior works, and escalates their demands over time.

This is genuinely debated. Some argue that in certain situations — particularly when you're facing a far more powerful opponent — making strategic concessions is not cowardice, it's pragmatism.

The careful distinction most analysts make is this: wise diplomacy and pragmatic negotiation are not the same as appeasement. The line is crossed into appeasement when:

  1. Your concessions reward aggression rather than address a legitimate grievance
  2. They encourage further demands rather than actually resolving the conflict
  3. You're giving in primarily out of fear, not out of genuine good-faith problem-solving

In other words, not every concession is appeasement — but every appeasement is a concession made to an aggressor that makes things worse in the long run.

• Appease (verb): "The company tried to appease angry customers by offering full refunds." — to satisfy or calm someone by giving them what they want
  • Appeaser (noun): a person who practices or advocates appeasement
  • Appeasing (adjective): "His appeasing tone failed to calm the crowd."

• "Historians widely regard the Munich Agreement as the ultimate failure of appeasement."
  • "Critics accused the prime minister of appeasement after she accepted all the rebel group's terms without negotiation."
  • "Giving in to every tantrum is a form of appeasement — it doesn't teach the child; it teaches them to demand more."
  • "The board warned that appeasement of an aggressive competitor would only delay the larger battle ahead."
  • "There's a thin line between flexible diplomacy and outright appeasement — the difference lies in whether you're rewarding aggression or resolving a genuine dispute."

Appeasement is the act of giving an aggressive or threatening party what they want in order to avoid conflict — a strategy widely regarded as short-sighted and dangerous, because it rewards aggression, invites more demands, and typically makes the eventual confrontation larger and worse than it would have been.
891:
An appeaser is a person who tries to avoid conflict or keep the peace by giving in to someone's demands — even when those demands are unfair, unreasonable, or threatening. Instead of standing firm or pushing back, an appeaser surrenders, makes concessions, or stays silent, hoping that satisfying the other person will calm them down or stop the problem.

The key idea is this: an appeaser doesn't necessarily agree with what the other person wants. They simply choose not to fight it, because they fear conflict more than they fear the consequences of giving in.
Why It Carries a Negative Meaning

The word appeaser is almost always used as a criticism. It implies that the person is:

  • Weak — lacking the courage to stand up for what is right
  • Short-sighted — thinking only about immediate peace, not long-term consequences
  • Enabling — by giving the aggressive party what they want, the appeaser actually encourages them to demand even more in the future

This is the central flaw of an appeaser: their strategy tends to backfire. Giving in to a bully rarely stops the bully — it often emboldens them.

Think of it this way: if a child throws a tantrum every time they want candy, and the parent gives in every single time just to stop the crying — that parent is acting as an appeaser. The child quickly learns that tantrums work, so the tantrums keep coming, and may even grow worse.

The most famous and important example of an appeaser in history is Neville Chamberlain, the British Prime Minister in the late 1930s. When Adolf Hitler began making aggressive territorial demands in Europe before World War II, Chamberlain chose not to confront him. Instead, in 1938, he agreed to let Hitler take a part of Czechoslovakia, believing this would satisfy Hitler and prevent a larger war. Chamberlain returned home famously declaring he had achieved "peace for our time."

It did not work. Hitler was not satisfied — he was encouraged. He continued expanding, and World War II began the very next year.

This episode burned the word appeaser into political vocabulary permanently. Today, when someone calls a political leader an appeaser, they are invoking this exact failure: the idea that tolerating or rewarding aggression only makes things worse.
How It's Used in Everyday Life

The word isn't limited to politics. You'll hear it in many ordinary situations:

  • A manager who never disciplines an employee who is rude to colleagues, just to avoid awkwardness, might be called an appeaser.
  • A person who always agrees with a domineering friend, even when the friend is clearly wrong, just to avoid an argument, is behaving like an appeaser.
  • A government that keeps making trade concessions to an unfair trading partner, hoping it will lead to goodwill, might be criticized as an appeaser.

In each case, the pattern is the same: someone with power or the ability to push back chooses not to, and instead gives the other party what they want.
Appeaser vs. Peacemaker — An Important Distinction

These two words might seem similar, but they describe very different people.

A peacemaker works to resolve conflict fairly — they bring both sides together, look for honest compromise, and try to find a solution where both parties are treated with dignity. A peacemaker is generally respected.

An appeaser, on the other hand, doesn't truly resolve anything. They simply hand over what the aggressive party wants to make the problem go away temporarily. There is no fairness, no honest compromise — just a one-sided surrender dressed up as peace.

This is why "appeasement" is considered a failure of strategy and courage, not an act of diplomacy.
Nuance: Can It Ever Be Neutral?

Occasionally, in very casual speech, someone might use "appeaser" loosely to describe any person who avoids confrontation or tries to keep everyone happy — without meaning it as a harsh criticism. For example, someone might jokingly describe themselves as "always the appeaser" in group disagreements, meaning they hate conflict and try to smooth things over.

But make no mistake: in serious contexts — political, historical, journalistic, or ethical — calling someone an appeaser is a sharp and deliberate insult. It accuses them of sacrificing principle for the sake of a fragile, temporary quiet.

An appeaser is someone who gives in to unreasonable or aggressive demands in order to avoid conflict, rather than standing their ground. The word carries a strong negative connotation, suggesting weakness, poor judgment, and a strategy that tends to make problems worse, not better. Rooted deeply in the political failures of the 1930s, it remains one of the most pointed criticisms you can level at a leader, an institution, or even an individual in any walk of life.
892: Appellate means relating to, or having the power to hear and decide, appeals in a legal context.
First, you need to understand what an "appeal" is

When a case is heard in a court, a judge (or a jury) makes a decision — someone wins, someone loses. But the losing side might believe that decision was wrong, not necessarily because the facts were wrong, but because the law was applied incorrectly, or because some serious procedural mistake was made during the trial.

That losing party can go to a higher court and say: "Please look at what the lower court did and correct the error." This formal request for a higher court to review a lower court's decision is called an appeal.

Everything connected to that review process is described by the word appellate.

The adjective "appellate" is almost always attached to a noun from the legal world. Here are the most important ones:

Appellate court — This is the big one, and the phrase you'll encounter most often. An appellate court is a court whose specific job is to review decisions made by lower courts. It is positioned above the trial court in the judicial hierarchy. The United States, for example, has a multi-layered system: trial courts at the bottom, then Courts of Appeals (the main appellate courts), and then the Supreme Court — the highest appellate court in the land. Most countries have a similar structure with trial courts below and appellate courts above.

Appellate jurisdiction — "Jurisdiction" means the legal authority a court has to hear a certain type of case. "Appellate jurisdiction" means the authority to review and decide appeals specifically. When a court has appellate jurisdiction over a case, it is legally empowered to examine what the lower court did. If a court does not have appellate jurisdiction over something, it simply cannot touch that case on appeal, no matter what.

Appellate judge / Appellate justice — A judge who sits on an appellate court. Their job is different from a trial judge; they are reviewing legal questions, not running a live trial.

Appellate brief — A formal written document that a lawyer submits to an appellate court, laying out the legal arguments for why the lower court's decision was right or wrong. It is the main way lawyers communicate their arguments to appellate judges.

Appellate review — The overall process of an appellate court examining a lower court's ruling.

Appellate procedure — The set of rules and steps that govern how an appeal must be handled — filing deadlines, required documents, oral argument rules, and so on.
The most important distinction: Trial courts vs. Appellate courts

This contrast is the heart of understanding "appellate." Burn this into your memory:

A trial court is where a legal dispute begins. Witnesses take the stand, evidence is presented, and the facts of the case are established ("Did the defendant run the red light? Yes or no?"). Trial courts deal with questions of fact. This is also called having original jurisdiction — the case originates there.

An appellate court does not hold a new trial. No new witnesses are called. No new evidence is introduced. The judges simply examine the written record from the trial below and listen to lawyers argue about legal questions: "Was the law applied correctly? Were the defendant's rights violated? Did the judge give the jury wrong instructions?" Appellate courts deal with questions of law, not questions of fact.

This is a rule of enormous importance: Appellate courts do not retry cases. They review them.

If the appellate court finds that a serious legal error occurred, it has a few options — it can overturn the lower court's decision entirely, modify it, or send the case back down to the trial court to be handled again (this is called "remanding" the case).
A note on how appellate courts make decisions

Unlike trial courts, appellate courts usually work in groups of judges, not a single judge alone. They read the written briefs, sometimes hear short oral arguments from the lawyers, and then deliberate together before issuing a written opinion explaining their decision and reasoning. These written opinions become a part of the law — they set precedent, meaning future courts are expected to follow the reasoning laid out in them.

"Appellate" is almost exclusively a legal term. You will encounter it in courtrooms, law school, legal journalism, and legal documents. It carries a formal, technical register. When you hear or read it, it is always signalling: we are no longer in the original, fact-finding stage of a dispute — we are now in the higher-level, law-reviewing stage.

• "She argued the case before the appellate court."
  • "The circuit court has appellate jurisdiction over decisions from the district courts below it."
  • "He spent his career in appellate law, writing briefs and arguing before courts of appeal."
  • "The appellate judges were unconvinced by the lower court's reasoning."
  • "After losing at trial, the company filed an appellate brief seeking to reverse the verdict."
  • "The matter was sent back to the trial court after the appellate court found a procedural error."
The one thing to always remember

Whenever you see "appellate," ask yourself: Is this about reviewing a decision already made by a lower court? If yes, "appellate" fits perfectly. The word always, without exception, lives in that space — the space between a decision already made and the higher authority empowered to examine it.
893:
An appellation is simply a name or title given to someone or something. When you call something by a particular name — whether that name is official, descriptive, or honorary — that name is its appellation.

Think of it this way: every person, place, and thing can have many names. Your full legal name, your nickname, your job title, a label someone gives you — all of these can be called appellations. The word is essentially a formal, precise way of saying "the name by which something is known or called."
How It Differs From the Simple Word "Name"

You might wonder: why not just say "name"? Great question.

"Name" is broad and neutral. "Appellation," on the other hand, carries a slightly more formal, deliberate, or significant feeling. It suggests that the name in question was consciously given, assigned, or recognized — often because it describes something meaningful about the person or thing being named.

  • Saying "Her name is Sarah" is plain and everyday.
  • Saying "She earned the appellation 'The Iron Lady'" tells you that this title was bestowed upon her because it meant something — it captured her character. It wasn't just a label; it was a significant designation.

So while every appellation is a name, not every name feels weighty enough to be called an appellation. The word implies that the name has some official standing, earned quality, or recognized importance.

• A fierce warrior king who was feared across the land might be given the appellation "The Conqueror."
  • A city loved for its jazz music might carry the appellation "The City of Music."
  • A scientist who changed the world might be honored with the appellation "The Father of Modern Physics."
  • Even a simple nickname can be called an appellation. If your friends always call you "Sparky," that is technically an appellation — it's the name by which you are known in that circle.

In all these cases, the appellation is more than a random label. It identifies the subject and often says something meaningful about them.
A Highly Important Specialized Use: Wine and Geography

The word "appellation" has a very well-known and precise legal meaning in the world of wine and food geography, and you will encounter it often in that context.

In this specialized sense, an appellation is an officially recognized and legally protected geographic name used to identify where a product — most commonly wine — comes from. The idea is that the specific land, soil, climate, and traditions of a region give its products a unique character that no other region can replicate. So the law steps in and protects that geographic name, ensuring only products genuinely from that region can carry it.

Classic examples:

  • Champagne is an appellation. It is a specific region in northeastern France. Sparkling wine made there, using specific grapes and methods, can legally be called "Champagne." Sparkling wine made anywhere else in the world — no matter how similar it tastes — legally cannot be called Champagne. It must use a different name (like "Prosecco," "Cava," or just "sparkling wine").
  • Bordeaux is an appellation — a wine-producing region in France. A wine labeled "Bordeaux" must come from grapes grown in that defined area.
  • Roquefort is an appellation for cheese — only blue cheese aged in the caves of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon in France can legally carry that name.

This system of protected geographic appellations is sometimes called an Appellation of Origin or, in French (since France pioneered this system), an Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée (AOC). Many countries have their own versions of this system. The United States uses the term American Viticultural Area (AVA) for its wine appellations (e.g., Napa Valley, Willamette Valley).

The key principle behind all of these is: the appellation guarantees authenticity and geographic origin. When you see it on a label, you know exactly where the product comes from — and that knowledge carries legal weight.

Understanding words that are close in meaning helps sharpen your grasp of a word.

  • Name — the broadest, most general option.
  • Title — often implies rank or honor (e.g., "Sir," "Doctor").
  • Designation — a name assigned for a specific purpose or category.
  • Label — often more informal; can sometimes feel reductive.
  • Moniker — casual or informal name.
  • Epithet — a descriptive name, often attached to a person's real name (e.g., "Alexander the Great" — "the Great" is an epithet).
  • Sobriquet — a nickname, usually affectionate or humorous.

Among all of these, "appellation" is the most formal and is the only one with a strong, legal specialized meaning in geography and food/wine.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Appellation" belongs to formal, literary, or professional writing and speech. You would not typically say it in casual conversation — that would sound stiff. You are more likely to encounter it in:

  • Academic or literary writing ("The poet went by the appellation 'Rumi.'")
  • Legal and regulatory documents (wine laws, food certification)
  • Journalism and formal criticism
  • History books

In casual speech, people simply say "name," "nickname," or "title." But when precision and formality matter, "appellation" is the right tool.

An appellation is a name or title — formal, earned, or legally recognized — by which a person, place, or thing is known, and in the world of wine and food, it specifically refers to a protected geographic name that guarantees a product's authentic regional origin.
894:
To append something means to add it to the end of something that already exists.

That's the heart of it. But there are two parts of this definition that deserve close attention, because they're what make "append" precise and distinct from simply saying "add."

Part 1: You are adding to something that already exists.
You aren't creating something new from scratch. There is already a document, a list, a file, a piece of writing — something that exists — and you are building onto it.

Part 2: You are adding to the end of it.
Not the beginning. Not the middle. The very end, after everything else that's already there.

So if you imagine a train already on the tracks, appending is like coupling a new carriage onto the very back of it. The train was already there, complete in itself, and you simply extended it at the tail end.

"Add" is a broad, general word. When you say you added something, it doesn't tell anyone where it went. Did it go at the start? In the middle? Somewhere random? No one knows.

"Append" is precise. It tells you exactly where the new thing went — at the end. This precision is why "append" is preferred in professional, technical, and formal situations where vagueness is a problem.
A Key Nuance: The Supplementary Nature of What's Appended

What you append is almost always secondary or supplementary in nature — meaning it supports, clarifies, or adds extra information to the main thing, but it isn't the main thing itself.

Think of it this way: the main content comes first and stands on its own. What you append is the extra material that follows it. An appended item is like a "P.S." at the bottom of a letter — it comes after the main body and adds something extra that didn't fit naturally within it.

In writing and documents:
This is one of the most common uses. A writer or professional might append a note, a clause, a signature, a disclaimer, or additional terms to the end of a document. For example: "Please append your signature at the bottom of the form." This means: write your signature at the end, after everything else.

In law and formal documents:
Legal documents frequently use "append." A contract might have additional schedules, conditions, or lists that are appended to it. These form what's often called an appendix (the noun form) — a section at the very end of a formal document that contains supplementary material. (Think of the appendix at the back of a textbook — it's named this way for exactly the same reason.)

In computing and programming:
This is where the word is used most heavily today. When working with files or data, to append means to add new data to the end of an existing file or list without touching or erasing what's already there.

For example, if a file contains the words Hello World and you append the word Today, it becomes Hello World Today. The original content is untouched; new content is simply added at the end.

In programming, lists and arrays have an "append" operation for exactly this purpose — adding a new item to the end of an existing list.

In everyday formal speech:
You might hear someone say, "I'd like to append a final remark to what was said earlier," meaning they want to add one last thing at the end of a discussion.

• It does not mean inserting something in the middle of existing content.
  • It does not mean replacing or overwriting existing content.
  • It does not mean adding something to the beginning.
  • It does not mean creating something new from nothing.

If any of those things are happening, "append" is the wrong word.

"Append" is a formal word. You won't hear it much in casual everyday conversation. In informal speech, people just say "add" or "tack on" or "attach." But in professional writing, legal documents, technical documentation, and programming, "append" is precise and natural. Knowing this word signals a level of professionalism and precision in your language.

QuestionAnswer

To append is to formally and precisely add something to the end of something that already exists, without disturbing what came before. The thing you append is typically supplementary — it adds to, clarifies, or extends the original. You'll encounter this word most in documents, legal texts, and technology. It is more precise than "add" because it specifies where the new material goes: always at the end.
895:
An appendage is something that is attached to a larger, more important main thing — and is considered secondary to it. It is not the center. It is not the core. It is the thing that hangs off the core, sticks out from it, or is connected to it.

Picture a tree trunk. The branches that grow out of it are appendages. The trunk is the main, central thing. The branches are attached to it, they grow out of it, and without it they would not exist — but they are not the trunk itself. That relationship is exactly what the word captures.

So if you want one clear sentence: an appendage is something attached to and extending from a larger main body, where it plays a supporting or secondary role rather than being the center of things.
In biology and the human body

This is where the word is used most naturally and most often. In biology, your arms, your legs, your hands, and your feet are all appendages of your body. A fish's fins are appendages. A cat's tail is an appendage. A crab's claws are appendages. An insect's antennae are appendages.

Notice what all of these have in common. They all extend outward from a central body. They all serve real, useful functions — your arms let you reach and carry things, a fish's fins help it steer through water, a cat's tail helps it balance. But none of them is the body itself. The body is the main thing. The appendage is what grows out of or attaches to that main thing.

A helpful image: think of a starfish. It has a central disc in the middle, and five arms radiating outward from it. Those five arms are appendages. The central disc is the core. Remove an arm, and the starfish is still fundamentally a starfish. Remove the central disc, and there is nothing for the arms to belong to.

The word "appendage" is also used to describe things, places, or even people that are attached to something larger in a non-physical sense — but the same idea applies. They are secondary, they depend on the main thing, and they are not the center.

For example, a small, powerless nation that has no real independence and is controlled entirely by a much larger and more powerful country might be described as an appendage of that country. It exists, it has a name, it has borders — but it functions entirely in the shadow of something bigger, as if it were just a limb attached to that country's body.

Similarly, a tiny department inside a huge corporation — one that has no real authority, no real budget, and no real influence over decisions — might be called an appendage of the company. It is technically part of the whole, but it is peripheral, not central.

And on a personal level, if someone constantly follows another person around, never acts independently, and seems to have no purpose or identity of their own, they might be called that person's appendage — as if they were simply an extension of the other person rather than their own individual.
The subtle tone: a hint of "lesser importance"

When the word is used figuratively (outside of a strict scientific context), it often carries a quiet undertone of dismissiveness. To call something an appendage is to gently suggest: this thing only exists in relation to something bigger, and on its own, it does not amount to much.

This is an important shade of meaning to understand. The word is not exactly an insult, but it is not neutral either. It positions the thing being described as dependent and secondary. Writers and speakers often reach for this word when they want to convey that something is not as important or as independent as it might appear or as it might like to be.

It is worth knowing that not everything that is part of something qualifies as an appendage. The word implies a few specific things that "part" does not.

First, an appendage typically extends outward or protrudes — it sticks out from the surface or edge of the main thing, rather than being buried deep inside it. Your heart is not an appendage. It sits at the very center of your body's function, it is hidden deep inside, and it is absolutely critical to life. Your pinky finger, on the other hand, qualifies perfectly as an appendage. It sticks out, it is attached at the outer reach of your hand, and while certainly useful, it is not what keeps you alive.

Second, an appendage has a degree of separateness from the core. You can often picture it being distinct, sticking out, almost as if it were added on. This is different from, say, your spine, which is deeply embedded in your body's structure and cannot be easily thought of as something "added on."

Third, and most importantly, an appendage is always less central and less important than the thing it is attached to. A part can be any portion of a whole — it could be the most important part. An appendage, by definition, is the lesser, outward-reaching portion.

An appendage is something that is attached to and extends from a larger, more important main body or thing. It is real, it is functional, and it genuinely belongs to the whole — but it is not the core. It exists at the edges, it sticks out, and it depends on the main thing for its context and its meaning. In biology, think of limbs, fins, tails, and claws. In everyday figurative use, think of anything — a place, an organization, a person — that exists in a permanently secondary, dependent relationship with something far bigger than itself.
896: The word appendix refers to something that is attached to or added onto something larger and more important — something that belongs to the main thing but is not the main thing itself. Think of it as a "hanger-on." The word has two common and distinct meanings depending on whether you're talking about the human body or a written document.

In anatomy (the study of the human body), the appendix is a small, narrow, finger-shaped pouch of tissue that is attached to the large intestine, located in the lower-right area of your abdomen. Its full name is the vermiform appendix, though people almost always just say "appendix."

What does it actually do? Honestly, scientists still debate this. For a long time, doctors believed the appendix was completely useless — a leftover from our evolutionary past with no function in modern humans. More recent research suggests it may play a minor role in the immune system, possibly helping to store beneficial gut bacteria. But here's the key point: the appendix is not essential. People who have it surgically removed live completely normal, healthy lives. You can function perfectly well without it.

The appendix becomes medically significant when it gets infected and inflamed, a condition called appendicitis. Appendicitis is a medical emergency. The inflamed appendix can swell up, cause severe pain (typically starting near the belly button and then shifting to the lower right side), and if left untreated, it can burst (rupture) — releasing harmful bacteria into the abdomen, which can be life-threatening. The standard treatment is surgical removal of the appendix, an operation called an appendectomy.

Example sentences:

  • "She was rushed to the hospital because her appendix had burst."
  • "The doctor confirmed it was appendicitis and scheduled an appendectomy."
Meaning 2: The Section at the End of a Book or Document

In the context of writing — books, research papers, reports, legal documents, academic theses — an appendix is a supplementary section placed at the very end of the main text. It contains material that is related to the main work but would be too detailed, too lengthy, or too disruptive to include in the body of the document itself.

Think of it this way: the author writes the main content in a clean, readable flow. But there's extra material — raw data, detailed charts, lengthy tables, survey questionnaires, technical calculations, lengthy legal citations, maps, glossaries, or supporting documents — that only some readers will want or need. Instead of cluttering the main text with all of this, the author moves it to the back and labels it the appendix (or if there are multiple such sections, Appendix A, Appendix B, and so on).

The appendix supports the main text but is not required reading to understand it. Readers can refer to it if they want more detail, but they won't miss the core argument or story if they skip it.

Example sentences:

  • "The survey questions used in the study can be found in Appendix B."
  • "Refer to the appendix at the back of the report for the full financial data."
  • "The novel included an appendix with maps of the fictional world."

Both meanings share the same underlying idea: something attached to or added onto something larger. The body's appendix is a small pouch attached to the intestine. A document's appendix is extra material attached to the end of a book. In both cases, the appendix is secondary — present and connected, but not the main event.

The word "appendix" has two accepted plural forms:

  • Appendices (pronounced uh-PEN-dih-seez) — the traditional, more formal plural, widely used in academic and professional writing. Preferred in British English.
  • Appendixes — a simpler, fully acceptable plural used in everyday American English.

Both are correct. When referring to body parts, you'll typically say "appendixes" (since people generally only have one, so the plural is rare). When referring to document sections, both "appendices" and "appendixes" are used, though "appendices" is more common in formal writing.

• Append (verb): To add something onto the end of something else. "Please append your signature to the form."
  • Appendage (noun): Something attached to a larger body — often used in biology to refer to limbs or attached structures.
  • Appendicitis (noun): The medical condition involving inflammation of the body's appendix.
  • Appendectomy (noun): The surgical operation to remove the appendix.

ContextWhat "appendix" means
Human bodyA small pouch attached to the large intestine; non-essential but can become dangerously infected
Books/documentsExtra supporting material placed at the end, beyond the main text

In short: whether it's a small organ in your belly or a section at the back of a book, an appendix is always something extra — attached, supplementary, and secondary to the main body it belongs to.
897: To appertain means to belong to, relate to, or be a natural and proper part of something.

When something appertains to something else, it means that first thing is connected to, belongs with, or is relevant to the second thing — usually in an official, natural, or inherent way.

Think of it as a formal way of saying "goes with," "belongs to," or "is part of."

The duties that appertain to the office of a judge must be carried out impartially.

Here, "the duties" naturally belong to and go with the role of a judge. They are inseparable from it.

Appertain carries two closely related senses:

1. To belong to something as a right, privilege, responsibility, or quality

This is the most common use. It says that something is a natural, proper, or inherent part of something else — especially a role, position, or ownership.

The rights appertaining to full citizenship were finally granted to them.
(Those rights belong with and go along with being a full citizen.)

With great power comes great responsibility — the two appertain to each other.
(They are inherently connected; one belongs with the other.)

The land, together with all privileges appertaining to it, was transferred to the new owner.
(All the privileges — fishing rights, access paths, etc. — that naturally go with owning that land.)

2. To be relevant or applicable to something

Here, "appertain" means that something has a connection to or bearing on a subject — it is relevant to it, it touches on it.

The committee will only discuss matters that appertain to the current investigation.
(Only matters relevant to, connected with, or bearing on the investigation.)

Please submit only documents appertaining to your application.
(Only documents that are relevant to or related to your application.)

This verb almost always works with the word "to". You say something appertains to something else. You will rarely (if ever) see it used without "to."

✅ responsibilities that appertain to the role
✅ matters appertaining to the case
❌ matters that appertain (feels incomplete)
The Tone and Register: Formal, Official, Sometimes Legal

Appertain is not a word you would use in everyday conversation. If a friend asks why you are cleaning the kitchen, you would not say "This duty appertains to me." You would just say "It's my job" or "It falls to me."

You encounter "appertain" mainly in:

  • Legal and official documents ("rights appertaining to ownership...")
  • Formal writing (academic papers, government texts, formal reports)
  • Literature, especially older or formal prose
  • Professional contexts where precision and gravity of language matter

It carries a sense of weight and seriousness. When a writer or lawyer uses "appertain," they are being deliberately precise — they want to communicate that the connection between two things is not casual or coincidental, but proper, inherent, and legitimate.
How It Relates to Similar Words

"Pertain to" is the most closely related word. The two mean almost the same thing, and in modern usage, "pertain to" is far more common. If you replace "appertain to" with "pertain to" in most sentences, the meaning stays intact. The difference is that "appertain" sounds slightly more elevated, archaic, or weighty.

matters pertaining to the case ← common and standard
matters appertaining to the case ← more formal, more old-fashioned

"Belong to" overlaps with the first sense of appertain — but "belong to" is simpler and broader. "Appertain to" specifically suggests a natural, inherent, or officially recognized belonging, often tied to roles, rights, or duties.

"Relate to" is a plain, everyday equivalent for the second sense — but again, "appertain to" is heavier and more formal.
A Summary to Lock It In

SituationWhat "appertain" is saying

When something appertains to a role, position, or thing, it is saying: this naturally belongs with it, goes with it, or is a proper and inherent part of it. When something appertains to a subject or matter, it is saying: this is relevant to it, connected to it, applicable to it.

Always formal. Always followed by "to." Always implying a real, substantive connection — not a vague or accidental one.
A Few More Examples Across Different Contexts

The ceremony concluded with a reading of all the rights and duties appertaining to the newly elected president.

He refused to answer questions that did not appertain to the matter at hand.

She inherited the estate along with all benefits and responsibilities appertaining thereto.
("thereto" is a formal word meaning "to it" — common in legal writing alongside "appertain")

The wisdom that appertains to old age cannot be rushed.
(The kind of wisdom that naturally belongs to and comes with old age.)

The word, in short, is a formal, precise, slightly old-fashioned verb for saying that something rightfully belongs to, is naturally connected to, or is relevant to something else. Use it when you want to sound authoritative and exact — and expect to see it most often in legal texts, formal documents, and careful literary writing.
898:
Appetency means a deep, natural, instinctive desire or craving for something. It's the kind of longing that doesn't feel like a choice — it feels like it comes from within you, almost like a built-in pull that your nature generates on its own.

Think of it this way: when a person who hasn't eaten all day walks past a bakery and feels an overwhelming urge toward food — that pull, that craving — is the spirit of appetency. But the word goes far beyond just hunger.
What Makes It Different From Just "Desire"

This is where things get interesting. "Desire" is a broad, everyday word. You can desire a new phone. You can desire a vacation. These are fairly conscious, surface-level wants.

Appetency is different in three important ways:

1. It is instinctive, not just chosen.
Appetency points to a craving that wells up from your deeper nature — something almost automatic. It's less "I've decided I want this" and more "something inside me is drawn to this."

2. It is persistent and deep-rooted.
It's not a passing whim. Appetency suggests a recurring, fundamental pull — something that keeps drawing you back. A person might have an appetency for solitude, meaning their nature consistently and naturally inclines them toward being alone.

3. It often carries a sense of natural necessity.
Philosophers and writers have used this word to describe the kinds of drives that living beings need to follow — drives tied to survival, growth, or their essential nature. An animal has an appetency for warmth. A curious mind has an appetency for knowledge.

Sense 1: A deep inner craving or longing (the most common use)

This is when appetency refers to a powerful, inborn desire that a person (or any living being) has — for something physical, intellectual, or emotional.

  • A child raised in silence might develop a profound appetency for music.
  • Some people carry an appetency for danger that no amount of caution can suppress.
  • She described her appetency for truth as the one constant of her life.

Notice how in each case, the desire feels rooted in the person's nature. It's not superficial.

Sense 2: A natural attraction or affinity between things (a more technical, philosophical use)

In a slightly different — and older — sense, appetency can describe the natural tendency of one thing to be drawn toward another, almost like magnetism. This was used in early philosophy and science to describe how certain substances or forces seem to "seek" each other out.

  • There is an appetency between iron and magnets.
  • Early philosophers spoke of the appetency of water to flow downward.

This second sense is rarely used in modern everyday writing, but you may encounter it in older texts or philosophical literature.
The Tone and Register of the Word

Appetency is a formal and literary word. You will not typically hear it in casual conversation. It belongs to the world of serious writing — philosophy, literary fiction, academic essays, or careful, elevated prose.

Using it signals that you are describing something with depth and gravity. It's not the word you'd use to say you want pizza tonight. It's the word you'd use to describe a lifelong, soul-level pull toward something — a calling, a compulsion, a fundamental drive.
How It Compares to Similar Words

WordKey Feel
  • Appetite — the everyday cousin of appetency; usually tied to food or basic physical wants. Less formal, less philosophical.
  • Craving — intense and often short-term; focused on a specific thing, often physical (a craving for chocolate, for sleep).
  • Yearning — emotional and often tinged with sadness or longing for something distant or unattainable.
  • Inclination — a gentle lean toward something; much weaker and milder than appetency.
  • Urge — sudden and impulsive; lacks the deep-rooted, natural quality of appetency.

Appetency sits in its own space: deep, natural, persistent, instinctive — and dignified enough to apply to the intellectual and spiritual dimensions of human life, not just the physical.

If you had to sum up appetency in one sentence, it would be:

Appetency is a powerful, natural, and deeply rooted craving or drive — one that feels like it comes from your very nature, not just a passing want.

And if you want a memory hook: think of "appetite," but dial it up — make it more philosophical, more persistent, more fundamental. Less "I want a snack" and more "I am drawn to this by something deep within me." That is appetency.
899:
Appetite is a natural desire or craving for something — most often food, but also for anything else that you want or enjoy deeply.

Think of it this way: when you smell something delicious cooking and you suddenly want to eat, that feeling is your appetite. It is not just about being physically empty — it is about the desire itself.

1. The literal meaning — food and eating

This is the most common use. Your appetite is your desire to eat.

  • When you are healthy and active, you usually have a good appetite — you feel like eating and enjoy your food.
  • When you are sick, stressed, or upset, you might lose your appetite — the desire to eat disappears, even if your body needs food.
  • After exercise, you often work up an appetite — physical effort makes your desire to eat grow stronger.

Notice that appetite is slightly different from hunger. Hunger is the raw physical signal your body sends — the rumbling stomach, the weakness. Appetite is the mental and emotional layer on top of that — the actual want, the anticipation, the pleasure of eating. You can be hungry without appetite (like when you're sick and your stomach is empty but food sounds terrible). You can also have appetite without being truly hungry (like when you see a dessert and feel like having it even though you just ate a full meal).

2. The extended meaning — desire for anything in life

This is where "appetite" becomes a very powerful and versatile word. It means a strong, natural craving or enthusiasm for any experience, idea, or thing — not just food.

  • An appetite for knowledge — a deep desire to learn and understand.
  • An appetite for adventure — a strong pull toward exciting, new experiences.
  • An appetite for power — an intense drive to control, lead, or dominate.
  • An appetite for risk — comfort with, and even enjoyment of, uncertain or dangerous situations.
  • An appetite for destruction — a craving to tear things down or cause harm.

In this sense, appetite suggests something that feels natural and recurring in a person — almost like a built-in hunger that keeps returning. It is not a one-time wish; it is a deep-seated tendency.

Appetite carries a sense of positive pull — something drawing you toward it, not pushing you away. It is desire that feels somewhat natural, not forced. This is why we say someone has "a healthy appetite" (for food or for life) — the word "healthy" fits naturally because appetite already feels like a normal, living urge.

It also carries a sense of capacity — how much you can take in, absorb, or enjoy. Someone with a big appetite for reading doesn't just like books; they consume them eagerly and in large amounts.
How Strong Can an Appetite Be?

Appetite ranges in intensity, and the English language has specific adjectives to describe this:

  • Good / healthy appetite — normal, strong desire; you enjoy eating or engaging with something.
  • Voracious appetite — extremely large and eager; almost greedy in its intensity. ("She has a voracious appetite for science fiction novels.")
  • Insatiable appetite — one that cannot be satisfied, no matter how much you feed it. ("His insatiable appetite for wealth led to his downfall.")
  • Poor / no appetite — little or no desire, often due to illness, sadness, or stress.

• "Whet someone's appetite" — to stimulate or increase someone's desire for something, not to satisfy it. ("The trailer whetted my appetite for the film." This means it made me more eager to watch it.)
  • "Lose one's appetite" — to stop feeling the desire to eat, usually because of strong emotions or illness.
  • "Work up an appetite" — to create hunger through physical activity or effort.
  • "Appetite suppressant" — something (like a drug or food) that reduces your desire to eat.
  • "Appetite for [something]" — the standard way to express craving in its extended sense.
Why This Word Feels Different from Similar Words

WordNuance
HungerThe raw physical sensation of needing food; more bodily and urgent
AppetiteThe desire and pleasure of wanting something; more mental and ongoing
CravingA strong, often sudden and specific urge (you crave chocolate, not food in general)
DesireBroad and general; can apply to almost anything, without the natural/physical connotation
YearningA deep, emotional longing — often for something distant or hard to reach

Appetite sits in a middle space: more refined than raw hunger, more natural and recurring than a sudden craving, and more specific and visceral than the abstract word "desire."

Appetite is about a natural, recurring desire — for food, for experience, for knowledge, for anything that feeds some part of you. It implies that the desire feels organic, not artificial. A person with appetite is alive, engaged, and drawn toward the world. A person without appetite is withdrawn, uninterested, perhaps unwell — in body or spirit.

That is why writers often use "appetite" when they want to show that someone is fully alive and hungry for life itself, not just for a meal.
